summary: This unit teaches you to make and bake the main pastries of a hotel or villa kitchen: short and sweet pastry, puff and rough puff, and choux. You will line and bake tart cases, make Jamaican gizzadas and beef patties, fill and finish pastries safely, and cool, store, label and present them. Food safety, allergens and temperatures run through every step.

blocks.p: This unit covers the pastry work of a hotel, villa or restaurant kitchen: from weighing the flour to labelling the finished tray. It is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees. Pastry is one of the most exact parts of cooking. The same flour, fat and water give a crumbly tart, a flaky patty or a hollow éclair, depending on **how cold, how much and how long** you work them.

Jamaican kitchens use pastry every day: the beef patty is the island's best-known snack, and the gizzada and the plantain tart are part of every bakery and bazaar. You will learn these alongside the classic pastries a hotel menu expects.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's kitchen. In practical work you make short pastry, gizzadas and baked-blind tart cases, then rough puff patties and choux. The assessor watches your hygiene, weighing, method, temperature checks, labelling and clean-up as well as the finished products.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph the food, your hands and the work area. Do not photograph a person's face unless they agree and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Pastry looks harmless, but meat patties, cream fillings and egg-based custards can make guests ill if they are handled badly. Pastry work is also full of heat, sharp tools and machines. Good habits protect the guest and you.

ul: Every food handler in Jamaica must hold a **Food Handler's Permit** from the local health department. Renew it as the department says.
Come to work clean, in a clean uniform and apron. Cover all your hair. Keep your nails short and clean, and take off rings, bracelets and watches (a plain wedding band only if the Centre allows it).

Wash your hands with soap and warm water for at least 20 seconds, and dry them with a clean paper towel: before you start, after handling raw meat or eggs, after touching your face, hair, phone or the bin, after the toilet, and after a break.
Cover a cut with a **blue waterproof plaster** and a glove. A blue plaster is easy to see if it falls into the food.
If you have vomiting, diarrhoea, a fever or an infected sore, tell your supervisor. Do not handle food until you are well and cleared to work.

head: Job
Typical safe figure
Why
rows: Cold storage of cream, custard, pastry cream, dairy fillings
5 °C or below
Germs grow slowly when it is cold.
Cooking a minced meat filling (core temperature)
About 74 °C
Kills harmful germs all through the meat. Check with a clean probe thermometer in the centre.
Keeping cooked patties hot for sale
About 63 °C or above
Hot enough to stop germs growing.
The danger zone
About 5 °C to 63 °C
Germs multiply fastest here. Do not leave food in this range longer than the Centre's food safety plan allows.

blocks.note: These figures are the usual teaching figures. Always follow the Centre's food safety plan and your instructor. Sanitise the probe before and after every use.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Keep raw meat, raw eggs and fish apart from pastry, cooked fillings and anything that will not be cooked again. Use separate boards and tools, colour-coded if your kitchen uses them.
Store raw meat on the lowest shelf, below ready-to-eat food, so that nothing drips onto it.
Do not use the same cloth for the work surface and for raw meat. Use clean cloths and change them often.
Do not taste with your fingers. Use a clean spoon each time.

blocks.p: An allergic reaction can be serious. You must know what is in every pastry and label it. Pastry products often contain these allergens:

head: Allergen
Where it is found in pastry work
rows: Cereals containing **gluten** (wheat)
All flour pastry: short, puff, choux, patties, gizzadas, tarts
**Milk**
Butter, milk, cream, pastry cream, butter glaze
**Eggs**
Egg wash, sweet pastry, choux, pastry cream, glazes
**Nuts**
Almond paste, nut toppings, praline, some fillings
**Sesame**
Seeds on rolls and some savoury pastries
**Soya**
Some margarines and shortenings
**Sulphites**
Dried fruit and some glazes

ul: Check the recipe and every ingredient label. If you are not sure, ask the chef. Never guess.
Wash your hands and clean the board and tools before making a product for a guest with an allergy, and keep it covered and apart.
Show the allergens on the label of every pastry you make for sale.

blocks.note: Lard is not an allergen, but some guests do not eat pork, and some do not eat any animal fat. Label the type of fat used, so that guests can choose.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Hazard
How you prevent harm
rows: Mixer
Fit the bowl and attachment properly and keep the guard on
Start on a low speed
Switch off and wait for it to stop before scraping or reaching in
Pastry sheeter (rollers)
Keep the guards on and hands clear of the rollers
Never clear a jam or clean it while it is running; switch off and unplug first
Oven and hot trays
Use **dry** oven gloves: heat passes quickly through wet cloth
Call 'hot tray' or 'behind you' when you carry one
Set hot trays down on a heat-proof surface, never on a plastic board
Hot sugar and hot fillings
Use a heavy pan, keep the handle turned in, stir with a long spoon
Hot sugar and boiling filling burn deeply: cool a burn under cool running water for at least 10 minutes and report it
Knives and cutters
Keep them on the board, away from the edge; wash them straight after use
Carry a knife point down; never try to catch a falling one
Flour and spills on the floor
Wipe up at once so that nobody slips.

blocks.note: Cool a burn under cool running water. Do not use ice, butter or toothpaste. Report every burn and cut and write it in the accident book.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Scrape off dough and crumbs
Wash with hot water and detergent
Rinse
Sanitise and leave for the contact time on the label
Dry or air-dry on a clean rack

blocks.p: Clean as you go. Leave the bench, the rolling pins, the cutters, the trays, the mixer and the floor clean, dry and ready for the next person. Never wipe a bench with the cloth that was used on raw meat.
Pastry is a chemistry job. Too much water makes it tough; too little makes it crack. That is why you weigh everything, and why you learn what each ingredient does.

head: Ingredient
Its job in pastry
Notes
rows: Flour
Gives the structure. Mixed with water, its proteins form **gluten**, a stretchy network.
Plain (soft) flour for short pastry: less gluten, so it stays tender
Strong (bread) flour, with more protein, for puff and choux: the layers and shells need to be strong
Fat (butter, margarine, shortening, lard)
Makes pastry **short** by coating the flour so gluten cannot grow too much. In puff pastry it keeps the layers apart.
Butter gives the best flavour and colour
Shortening and lard give a very short, crumbly pastry
Fat must be cold for short and puff pastry
Water (or milk)
Binds the dough together. In puff and choux it turns to steam and lifts the pastry.
Use cold, a little at a time
Too much makes the pastry tough and shrunk
Salt
Flavour; it also strengthens the dough a little.
A pinch in sweet and savoury pastry.
Sugar
Sweetness, tenderness and browning, mainly in sweet pastry.
Caster or icing sugar dissolves best.
Eggs
Enrich and bind sweet pastry; in choux they hold the air and set the shell. Egg wash gives a golden shine.
Use clean, uncracked eggs within date.
Raising agent
Not used in plain pastry. The lift comes from **steam** and layers.
Do not confuse pastry with cake or bread.

ul: Weigh flour, fat and sugar in **grams**. A cup of flour can differ by 30 g or more, depending on how it is packed.
Weigh or measure the water exactly. The amount of liquid decides whether the pastry is tender, tough or crumbly.
Scale a recipe up or down by keeping the ratios the same. Example: a recipe uses 200 g flour and 100 g fat. For 600 g flour, multiply everything by 3: 300 g fat.
Keep all fat and water cold, and the work area cool. In Jamaican heat, work early in the day or in an air-conditioned room if you can, and chill the bowl, the pin and even the flour on hot days.

blocks.note: Mise en place means having everything in its place before you start: recipe read, allergens listed, ingredients weighed, tins prepared, oven on, tools clean. A pastry cook who stops halfway to look for a tin lets the fat warm up and ruins the dough.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: Jamaica's power supply is 110 V at 50 Hz, with 220 V for some heavy equipment. Check that a mixer or sheeter is made for its socket, keep cables off wet floors and report any damaged plug.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Short** pastry is crumbly and tender, not tough. It is 'short' because the fat has coated the flour and kept the gluten short. It is the base of tart cases, pies and gizzadas.

Plain short pastry uses **half as much fat as flour** (a 2 : 1 ratio), a pinch of salt and just enough cold water to bind. Example: 400 g flour, 200 g fat, a pinch of salt and about 4 to 6 tablespoons of cold water.

flow: Weigh the flour, fat and salt; chill the fat and water
Sift the flour and salt into a cool bowl
Cut the cold fat into small cubes and add it
Rub in with the fingertips, lifting the mix so that it stays cool and takes in air, until it looks like fine breadcrumbs
Add cold water a little at a time, mixing with a palette knife until the dough just comes together
Gather the dough lightly: do not knead it
Wrap it, label it and rest it in the fridge for at least 30 minutes

ul: **Keep everything cool**: cool hands, cold fat, cold water, a cool bench. Warm fat melts into the flour and the pastry turns greasy and hard.
**Handle it as little as possible**: overworking develops gluten and makes the pastry tough.
**Add water a little at a time**: too much water makes it sticky and tough, and it shrinks in the oven.
**Rest it**: resting relaxes the gluten, firms the fat and stops shrinking.
Roll lightly and evenly, in one direction, turning the pastry a quarter turn often. Use only a little flour on the bench.

blocks.p: Sweet pastry has sugar and egg. It is often made by the **creaming method**: beat the soft butter and icing sugar together, beat in the egg, then mix in the flour until it just forms a dough. It is crisper and finer than plain short pastry, and is used for fruit tarts and tartlets. Wrap it and rest it well, because it is soft and sticky when new.

head: Point
Short pastry
Sweet pastry
rows: Sugar
None, or very little
Yes, usually icing or caster sugar
Egg
No
Yes: gives a crisp, fine texture
Method
Rubbing-in
Often creaming, or rubbing-in
Used for
Savoury pies, gizzadas, quiches
Fruit tarts, tartlets, sweet flans

flow: Lightly flour the bench and the pin
Roll the rested pastry evenly to about 3 mm thick, a little larger than the tin
Roll it loosely around the pin and lift it over the tin
Ease it into the base and corners without stretching it, and press it gently against the sides
Trim the top edge with a knife or by rolling the pin across the rim
Prick (dock) the base with a fork
Rest the lined case in the fridge before baking

blocks.p: **Do not stretch the pastry** when you line a tin: stretched pastry pulls back and shrinks when it bakes. Always lift and ease it in.

**Baking blind** means baking a pastry case before it is filled. You do it when the filling is wet (pastry cream, custard) or needs little cooking (fresh fruit, a cold filling). It stops the base going soggy.

flow: Line the chilled case with baking paper, pressing it into the corners
Fill it with baking beans or rice, right up to the top of the sides
Bake in a preheated oven (about 180–200 °C, as the recipe and oven maker say) until the edges are set
Lift out the paper and beans
Bake a few minutes more until the base is dry and lightly golden
Cool on a wire rack before filling

ul: The paper and beans stop the base from rising and the sides from falling in.
Pricking (docking) lets steam escape so that the base does not bubble up.
For a very wet filling, brush the hot base with a little beaten egg and return it to the oven for a minute to seal it.

head: Fault
Likely cause
How to prevent it
rows: Tough, hard pastry
Overworked; too much water; too much flour on the bench
Handle lightly, add water slowly, use little extra flour
Shrinks in the tin
Stretched when lining; not rested; rolled too thin
Lift and ease in; rest before baking; roll to 3 mm
Too crumbly, breaks when rolled
Too little water; fat not rubbed in finely; too much fat
Add water slowly to bind; check the amounts
Soggy, pale base
Not baked blind; wet filling; oven too cool
Bake blind; cool the filling; preheat the oven
Greasy, heavy
Warm hands or warm fat; oven too cool
Keep everything cold; preheat the oven
Uneven colour
Uneven rolling; hot spots in the oven
Roll evenly; turn the tray during baking

blocks.note: If short pastry cracks when you roll it, do not add more water. Press the edges together and rest it a few minutes at room temperature. Over-wetting makes it tough.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Three pastries every Jamaican baker must know are the gizzada, the beef patty and the plantain tart. Each uses a pastry from this unit, and each has its own food safety points.
A **gizzada** is a small tart with a pinched, frilled shell of short pastry and a filling of sweet, spiced grated coconut. It is sold in bakeries and at bazaars across the island.

flow: Make a short pastry (a firm one, as for tarts) and rest it in the fridge
Cook the filling: grated coconut with brown sugar, grated nutmeg, ginger, a little butter and vanilla, in a pan with a little water, stirring, until thick and sticky
Cool the filling completely
Roll the pastry thinly, about 3 mm, and cut rounds with a cutter
Pinch the edge of each round all the way round to make the frilled rim, and place on a lined tray
Fill each shell with the coconut filling
Bake until the pastry is crisp and golden, at the heat the recipe and oven maker say
Cool on a wire rack; label with name, date and allergens (wheat, milk)

ul: Cook the filling until it is thick. A loose filling runs over and makes a mess.
Cool it first. A hot filling melts the fat in the pastry.
Some recipes bake the shells partly before filling. Follow the Centre's recipe.

blocks.p: A Jamaican **beef patty** is a half-moon of yellow, flaky pastry filled with spiced minced beef. The yellow colour comes from **turmeric or curry powder** in the dough. A rough puff or flaky pastry gives the best texture.

flow: Make the pastry coloured with turmeric or curry powder, and chill it
Cook minced beef with onion, scallion, thyme, garlic, Scotch bonnet pepper and seasoning until cooked through
Check the core temperature with a clean probe thermometer: about 74 °C, or as the Centre's food safety plan says
Add breadcrumbs to bind and soak up the fat
Cool the filling quickly in a shallow tray, cover and chill it
Roll the pastry thinly and cut rounds
Put cold filling on one half, brush the edge with water or egg, fold over and crimp with a fork
Make a small steam vent, egg-wash the top and bake until golden and crisp
Serve hot, or keep hot in a warmer at about 63 °C or above

head: Point
Why it matters
rows: Cool the filling before it goes into the pastry
Hot filling melts the fat, so the pastry is greasy and not flaky; it also warms the dough into the danger zone.
Do not overfill and seal the edge well
Too much or wet filling bursts the patty and leaks during baking.
Egg-wash the top only
Egg wash on the cut edge glues the layers and stops the rise.
Keep raw mince apart from the pastry and wash your hands after handling it
Raw meat carries germs that must not reach ready-to-eat food.
Hold hot or chill
Patties not sold at once must be kept at 63 °C or above, or cooled quickly and chilled, then reheated until piping hot.

blocks.note: Scotch bonnet pepper burns the skin and the eyes. Wear gloves when you cut it, do not touch your face, and wash your hands well afterwards. Pepper oil stays on the skin for hours.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A **plantain tart** is a short pastry case or a folded half-moon (a **turnover**) filled with ripe, sweet plantain that has been boiled or fried, mashed and flavoured with sugar and spices. Cook and cool the filling first, then fill and bake until the pastry is golden. A turnover is made by folding a round of pastry in half over the filling and crimping the edge, like a patty.

blocks.note: Jamaican pastry shops sell patties, gizzadas and tarts by the dozen for bazaars, sports days and church functions. Order quantities need scaling up, so work the weights out first, plan the baking in batches, and label every tray so that nothing is mixed up at the event.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Puff, rough puff and other laminated pastry

blocks.p: Puff pastry rises into hundreds of crisp, flaky layers. It is made by trapping layers of fat between layers of dough, called **laminating**. In the oven the water in the dough and fat turns to steam. The steam is trapped between the layers and pushes them apart, and the fat stops them sticking together.

ul: A dough of strong flour, salt and cold water, with a block of cold butter or pastry fat of **about the same weight as the flour**.
Rest the dough, roll it into a square, and wrap the fat inside it like an envelope.
Roll the parcel into a long rectangle, always in one direction, and fold it in three (a single turn) or four (a double turn).
Rest in the fridge between turns so that the fat stays firm and the dough relaxes.
Classic puff has six single turns (or the same with double turns). The more turns, the thinner the layers, up to a point.
The fat and the dough should be about the same firmness. Fat that is too hard breaks through the dough; fat that is too soft melts in.

blocks.p: **Rough puff** is the quick version. Lumps of fat are mixed into the dough without rubbing in, then the dough is rolled and folded three or four times. It uses less fat (about three-quarters of the weight of the flour), gives fewer layers, and is ideal for patties, pies and sausage rolls.

head: Point
Full puff
Rough puff
rows: Fat to flour
About equal weight
About three-quarters
Fat added
As a block wrapped in the dough
In lumps mixed into the dough
Turns
About six
About three or four
Time
Long; several rests
Short
Rise
Tall, even layers
Lower, flakier
Used for
Vol-au-vents, palmiers, high tart tops
Patties, pies, sausage rolls

ul: Cut with a **sharp** cutter or knife, pressing straight down. A blunt cutter or a sawing cut squashes the edges together, and the layers cannot rise.
Brush **egg wash on top only**, not down the cut edges. Egg on the edges glues the layers shut and stops the rise.
Chill the cut shapes before baking. Cold fat melts slowly and makes more steam.
Bake in a hot, preheated oven, about 200–220 °C as the recipe and oven maker say. Do not open the door early, because cold air can make the pastry sink.
Use scraps carefully: stack them (do not ball them up), rest them and re-roll once. Pastry from scraps rises less.

head: Fault
Likely cause
Prevention
rows: Uneven or lopsided rise
Rolled unevenly; blunt cutter; egg wash on the edges
Roll evenly; cut straight down with a sharp cutter; glaze the top only
Fat leaks out in the oven
Pastry too warm; fat broke through; oven too cool
Chill between turns; preheat the oven
Little rise, heavy
Too few turns; fat too soft; dough rolled too thin
Keep it cold; fold correctly; rest well
Tough pastry
Dough not rested; too much flour worked in
Rest between turns; brush off extra flour
Shrinks after cutting
Stretched during rolling; not rested
Roll gently; rest before cutting and baking

ul: **Vol-au-vent** (and the small **bouchée**): a round puff case with a hollow centre, filled with a savoury filling in a sauce.
**Palmiers**: sugared puff rolled to the middle from both sides, sliced and baked.
**Sausage rolls, cheese straws and patties**: savoury items from puff or rough puff.

**Filo (phyllo)** is not puff pastry: it is made of paper-thin sheets, each brushed with butter, layered for strudel and baklava. Keep unused sheets covered with a damp cloth, or they dry out and crack.

blocks.note: Working with butter-rich pastry in a hot Jamaican kitchen needs planning. If the dough gets soft and sticky, stop, wrap it and chill it for 20 minutes. Never add more flour to cure stickiness: chill it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Choux** pastry is different from all the others. It is **cooked in a pan first** and then beaten with eggs into a smooth paste. It is piped, and in the oven the water in the paste turns to steam and puffs it into a hollow shell. It is used for éclairs, profiteroles and cream puffs.

A common recipe is 250 ml water, 100 g butter, a pinch of salt, 150 g strong or plain flour and about 4 medium eggs (about 200 ml, beaten). Recipes differ: follow the Centre's recipe. The eggs are added a little at a time until the paste is right, not by a fixed count.

flow: Heat the water, butter and salt in a pan until the butter has melted and the water boils
Take the pan off the heat and add all the sifted flour at once
Beat hard with a wooden spoon until smooth
Return to a low heat and beat until the paste forms a ball and leaves the sides of the pan clean
Cool the paste a little, so that it will not cook the eggs
Beat in the beaten eggs a little at a time, beating smooth after each addition
Stop when the paste is smooth and shiny, and drops slowly from the spoon
Pipe onto a lined tray: fingers for éclairs, small mounds for profiteroles
Bake in a hot oven without opening the door at first, until well risen, golden and dry
Make a small hole in each to let the steam out, and cool on a rack

head: Point
Why
rows: Boil the water and butter together, so the butter melts before the water boils away
Too much boiling off changes the amount of water, and the paste will not puff.
Add all the flour at once
The flour cooks evenly and no lumps form.
Cool the paste before adding the egg
Hot paste scrambles the egg.
Add the egg gradually
The right consistency is more important than the number of eggs.
Do not open the oven early
The shell is not yet set, and cold air makes it collapse.
Bake until dry and crisp
A shell that is not dry inside will go flat when it comes out.
Make a hole to let the steam out
Trapped steam makes the shell soft.

blocks.p: A typical oven plan is a hot oven (about 200–220 °C) for the first 10 to 15 minutes to make the shells rise, then a lower heat (about 180 °C) to dry them. Always use the recipe and oven maker's instructions.

head: Fault
Likely cause
rows: Flat, soft buns that sink after baking
Taken out too soon; shells not dry; oven door opened early
Do not rise
Paste too thin, or too stiff; oven too cool; flour not cooked in the pan
Cracked, uneven shapes
Oven too hot at the start; uneven piping
Paste runs and spreads
Too much egg
Paste is stiff and lumpy
Too little egg, or egg added too fast

ul: Fill cold, cooled shells with chilled whipped cream or **pastry cream** (crème pâtissière), using a clean piping bag.
Éclairs are often topped with chocolate or fondant; profiteroles are served with chocolate sauce.
Fill as close to service as you can. Filled choux go soft after a few hours, and cream fillings need to stay chilled.
Choux with cream fillings must be stored covered in the fridge at 5 °C or below, or as the Centre's food safety plan says.

blocks.note: The choux pan and the paste are very hot. Use a long spoon, keep the handle turned in, and do not lean over the pan: boiling water splashes.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Cook meat and vegetable fillings fully, drain off extra liquid and fat, and **cool them before they go into pastry**.
Wet fillings make soggy pastry and burst patties. Thicken them or add a binder such as breadcrumbs.
Cool quickly: spread in a shallow tray, cover loosely, and chill. A deep pot of filling stays warm in the middle for hours.
Keep raw meat, cooked filling and pastry apart while you work.
Cooked fruit or plantain fillings are cooled before use.
Fresh fruit is put on a baked-blind case close to service, often with a glaze so that it shines and does not dry out.
Coconut, spices and brown sugar make the typical Jamaican sweet fillings.

blocks.p: Pastry cream is a thick, smooth cream used in éclairs, tarts and fruit flans. It is made with milk, egg yolks, sugar, a little flour or cornflour, and vanilla.

flow: Heat the milk with the vanilla until nearly boiling
Whisk the egg yolks, sugar and flour or cornflour in a bowl
Whisk in the hot milk, then pour it back into the pan
Stir all the time over a medium heat until it boils and thickens
Cook it for a minute or two, so that the flour is cooked and there is no floury taste
Pour it into a clean, shallow tray and cover with cling film touching the surface, to stop a skin forming
Chill quickly at 5 °C or below

ul: Pastry cream is a **high-risk food**: milk and eggs let germs grow quickly if it is left warm.
Use clean piping bags. Never refill a used bag with fresh filling.
Use it within the time the Centre's food safety plan allows, and label it with the date.

head: Finish
How and when
rows: Egg wash (egg beaten with a little milk or water)
Brushed on top before baking, for a golden shine. Contains **egg**: list the allergen.
Milk wash
A lighter finish with less colour.
Butter glaze
Brushed on after baking for a soft top.
Apricot or fruit glaze
Heated and brushed over fruit tarts so that they shine.
Icing sugar
Dusted just before service, or it melts and dissolves.
Chocolate or fondant
For éclairs, once they are cool.
Crimping (fluting)
Pressing or pinching the edge of a pie or patty to seal it and make a pattern.
Steam vent
A small hole or cut in the top of a pie, so that steam can escape.

blocks.note: Seal pies and patties carefully. If the edge is not sealed, the filling leaks out in the oven, and the product looks careless.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Cool baked pastry on a **wire rack**, so that steam escapes and the base stays dry and crisp.
Do not fill or wrap pastry until it is completely cool: warm pastry makes the filling sweat and the pastry soggy.
Cool fillings quickly in shallow trays (see above).

head: Product
How to store it
rows: Unbaked pastry dough
Wrapped, labelled and chilled for the next day; or frozen for longer.
Baked, unfilled tart cases
In an airtight tin, in a cool dry place, until close to service.
Cream or custard pastries (éclairs, filled tarts)
Covered, in the fridge at 5 °C or below, or as the Centre's food safety plan says.
Beef patties (cooked)
Kept hot at about 63 °C or above; otherwise cooled quickly, chilled, and reheated until piping hot.
Gizzadas and dry pastries
Airtight container, cool and dry, away from pests.
Raw meat fillings
Lowest shelf of the fridge, covered, apart from other foods.

blocks.p: Every container or tray of stock carries a label with the **product name, the date made, a use-by date and the allergens**. Stock is used in date order: **first in, first out** (FIFO). Throw out anything past its date or that has been kept too long in the danger zone.

ul: Make pastries of **equal size and shape**: they look neat, the portions are fair, and the cost can be controlled.
Arrange them in tidy rows on clean trays, with sweet and savoury apart.
Handle with tongs, gloves or a clean spatula: never bare hands.
Each tray carries a label with the product name and its allergens.
Keep cream pastries chilled on a cold display, and hot patties hot, until service.
Finish items just before service: dust icing sugar, glaze fruit, fill choux.

blocks.p: Plan a mixed tray with variety and balance: for example, gizzadas, fruit tarts, éclairs and small patties, with the sweet and savoury items kept apart.

ul: Weigh and portion to the recipe: the cost of each pastry is worked out from the recipe, so every one that is too big costs the kitchen money.
Use pastry trimmings sensibly (for example, in pie lids or cheese straws, where the recipe allows).
Record waste, so that the team can reduce it.
Clean, sanitise and put away all tools and equipment, as in the cleaning-down steps earlier.
Switch off and unplug mixers and the sheeter; make sure the oven is off.
Report faulty equipment, low stock and any accidents to your supervisor.
I can explain why a food handler needs a Food Handler's Permit, and list the rules of personal hygiene.
I can name the safe temperatures: 5 °C or below for cream, about 74 °C core for a meat filling, and 63 °C or above for hot holding.
I can prevent cross-contamination between raw meat, eggs and pastry.
I can list the allergens in common pastries and label them.
I can use mixers, sheeters, ovens and hot sugar safely.
I can say what flour, fat, water, salt, sugar and eggs do in pastry.
I can name the main types of pastry and their methods.
I can weigh accurately, scale a recipe and plan my mise en place.
I can make short pastry by the rubbing-in method and give the rules for keeping it short.
I can roll out, line a tin, dock and bake blind.
I can find the cause of a fault in short pastry and say how to prevent it.
I can make a gizzada and a beef patty, and explain the food safety steps for the filling.
I can make rough puff or puff pastry, and explain why it rises in layers.
I can cut, glaze and bake puff pastry for an even rise.
I can make choux paste, bake it until dry, and fill and finish éclairs and profiteroles.
I can make pastry cream and cool and store it safely.
I can cool, store, label, portion and present a tray of pastries.
I can clean down and put away my tools and equipment.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step, not only the step. For example: 'I rest the pastry in the fridge so that the gluten relaxes and the fat firms, so that it does not shrink in the oven.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: A crumbly, tender pastry made by rubbing fat into flour; fat is half the weight of the flour.
Rubbing cold fat into flour with the fingertips until it looks like fine breadcrumbs.
A short pastry with sugar and egg, often creamed; crisp and fine.
The stretchy network formed when flour proteins meet water.
Folding fat into dough in layers, as in puff pastry.
A quick puff pastry with lumps of fat mixed into the dough.
A pastry cooked in a pan, then beaten with eggs, which puffs into a hollow shell.
Paper-thin sheets of pastry layered with butter.
Baking a pastry case before it is filled, lined with paper and baking beans.
Pricking the base of pastry with a fork so that steam escapes.
Chilling pastry so that the gluten relaxes and the fat firms.
Beaten egg, with a little milk or water, brushed on for a golden shine.
Pinching or pressing the edge of a pastry to seal and decorate it.
A small hole in the top of a pie so that steam escapes.
A Jamaican tart with a pinched shell and a spiced coconut filling.
A Jamaican half-moon pastry with a yellow crust and spiced beef filling.
A pastry made by folding a round over a filling.
A thick custard of milk, egg yolks, sugar and flour used to fill pastries.
The temperature at the centre of the food, checked with a probe.
The range of about 5 °C to 63 °C in which germs grow fast.
Germs passing from raw to ready-to-eat food.
A substance that can cause a harmful reaction in some people, such as gluten, milk, egg, nuts and sesame.
First in, first out: using the oldest stock first.
Having everything prepared and in its place before you start.

c1.title: Patties for sports day in Old Harbour
c1.text: Trainees Shanice and Dwayne are making 200 beef patties for a primary school sports day in Old Harbour that starts at 11:00 a.m. The yellow rough puff pastry is chilled. Shanice has cooked the minced beef, onion, scallion, thyme and Scotch bonnet filling; her probe thermometer reads 68 °C in the centre. Dwayne, who is behind time, wants to spoon the steaming filling straight from the pan onto the pastry rounds. Shanice has just handled the raw mince.

c2.title: Tart cases in the Mandeville training kitchen
c2.text: A class in the Centre's kitchen in Mandeville makes sweet short pastry for fruit tarts filled with chilled pastry cream. Odane stretches his pastry to make it fit the tin and bakes the case straight away without baking blind. Keisha rolls hers to 3 mm, lifts it in without stretching, pricks the base, rests it, then lines it with paper and beans. The next day, Odane's case has shrunk away from the sides and the base is pale and soft once filled.

c3.title: Gizzadas for a church bazaar in Savanna-la-Mar
c3.text: Miss Verona Pinnock orders 150 gizzadas for a church bazaar in Savanna-la-Mar on Saturday. Trainee Rohan makes the short pastry, rolls it to 3 mm, and cuts rounds. He spoons in warm, loose coconut filling, and some of the shells burst in the oven and leak. He pinches the rims of the next trays after the filling has cooled and thickened, and these bake well. Miss Pinnock asks what is in the gizzadas, because one of her helpers cannot eat gluten or dairy.

c4.title: Éclairs for a hotel function in Negril
c4.text: Trainee Tamika bakes éclairs for a hotel lunch in Negril. She adds all the beaten egg to the hot choux paste at once, and the paste runs off the spoon. Her first tray bakes flat. On the second try she cools the paste, adds the egg slowly until it drops slowly from the spoon, and opens the oven door after 8 minutes to check. The éclairs sink a little. She fills the finished éclairs with pastry cream and leaves the tray on the bench for the 12:30 service, at about 30 °C in the kitchen.

c5.title: Puff pastry in a hot Kingston kitchen
c5.text: At the Centre's kitchen in Kingston, Marlon is making puff pastry for vol-au-vent cases on a hot afternoon. The butter becomes soft and greasy while he rolls. After the first turn he goes on straight away with the next turn. He cuts the cases with a blunt cutter, brushes egg wash over the tops and down the cut edges, and bakes them. They rise lopsided and some leak butter onto the tray.

questions.q: Shanice's probe reads 68 °C in the middle of the filling. What should she do?
o: Keep cooking and check again until it reads about 74 °C
Take it off the heat, because the breadcrumbs will cook it in the oven
Record 68 °C, since the filling is already hot enough to use
Stir in a little cold water, so the filling cooks through more evenly
questions.why: A minced meat filling must reach about 74 °C at its core, or the temperature in the Centre's food safety plan, to kill harmful germs. 68 °C is not enough, and the oven will not reliably finish it once it is inside pastry.

questions.q: Why is Dwayne's plan to put steaming filling straight onto the pastry a poor one?
o: The filling would lose its flavour once it is inside the cold pastry
The hot filling melts the fat, so the pastry is greasy
The pastry would not be strong enough to hold the weight of the filling
The turmeric in the pastry reacts badly with the heat of the meat
questions.why: Hot filling melts the cold fat that makes rough puff flaky, and warms the dough into the danger zone. Cool the filling first, in a shallow tray, so that the patties bake flaky and safe.

questions.q: What is the best way to cool the cooked filling quickly?
o: Leave it in the deep pot on the bench with the lid off
Stir cold water into it until it stops steaming
Cover the hot pot and put it straight into the fridge
Spread it in shallow trays, cover it and chill it
questions.why: A thin layer cools fast and gets through the danger zone quickly. A deep pot stays warm in the middle for hours, and a hot pot in the fridge warms everything beside it.

questions.q: Shanice has just handled the raw mince. What must she do before she touches the pastry?
o: Wipe her hands on her apron, as the mince is going to be cooked anyway
Rinse her hands under the tap and dry them on the work cloth
Wash them with soap and warm water, then use a paper towel
Put on a glove over her unwashed hands and carry on
questions.why: Raw meat carries germs that must not be passed on to pastry or other food. Handwashing with soap and warm water, then drying on a clean paper towel, removes them; a glove over dirty hands only spreads them.

questions.q: Why has Odane's tart case shrunk away from the sides of the tin?
o: He rolled the pastry too thick, so it pulled itself inwards in the oven
He stretched the pastry into the tin, and it pulled back as it baked
He used cold butter, which makes the pastry contract in the hot oven
He pricked the base, so the sides had nothing to hold them up
questions.why: Stretched pastry pulls back as it bakes. Lift the pastry in and ease it into the corners without stretching, and rest the lined case before baking.

questions.q: What probably made the base of Odane's tart pale and soft once it was filled?
o: The tin was greased too lightly before the pastry went in
The pastry cream was chilled before it went into the case
He did not bake the case blind before filling it
He rolled the pastry too thin, so the filling went through it
questions.why: A wet filling like pastry cream soaks into an unbaked or half-baked base. Baking blind first dries and sets the case so that it stays crisp.

questions.q: Keisha lines her case with baking paper and fills it with baking beans. What is this for?
o: It stops the base rising and the sides slumping while the case sets
It flavours the pastry with the beans while the case is baking
It keeps the pastry soft so that the filling can soak in later
It makes the case cook faster by holding the oven heat in
questions.why: The weight of the beans on the paper holds the pastry down and keeps the sides upright until the case is set. The paper and beans are lifted out for the last few minutes to dry the base.

questions.q: Keisha's pastry cream will go into the baked case. How should the filled tarts be stored before service?
o: In a covered tin on the shelf, to keep the pastry crisp until service
Covered, in the fridge at 5 °C or below, as the food safety plan says
On the bench under a cloth until the guests arrive for the meal
In the warm cupboard, so that the cream does not form a skin on top
questions.why: Pastry cream is made with milk and eggs, so germs grow fast in it if it is warm. Keep filled tarts covered and chilled, and use them within the time the Centre's plan allows.

questions.q: Some of Rohan's first gizzadas burst and leak in the oven. What was the most likely cause?
o: The pastry was rolled to 3 mm instead of thicker
The pastry was rested too long in the fridge before rolling
The filling was warm and loose, and the shells overfull
The oven was heated before the gizzadas went in
questions.why: A warm, loose filling runs and bursts the shell, and it melts the fat in the pastry. Cook the filling until thick and sticky, cool it, and do not overfill.

questions.q: Which part of the gizzada gives it its traditional shape?
o: A rim pinched all the way round the filled round of pastry
A lid of pastry sealed over the top of the filling
A coil of pastry laid around the edge of a flat round
A rim cut flat with a sharp knife and brushed with egg
questions.why: A gizzada is a small, open tart with a frilled rim pinched round the shell, and a sweet, spiced coconut filling.

questions.q: Miss Pinnock's helper cannot eat gluten or dairy. What should Rohan do?
o: Tell her gizzadas are safe, as they have no cheese in them
Check the recipe, tell her it has wheat and butter, and label it
Offer her the filling without the pastry, as it is only coconut
Say that the dairy is only a little butter, so it will not matter
questions.why: Gizzada pastry contains wheat (gluten) and usually butter (milk), and the filling often has butter too. Tell the customer honestly, and label allergens on everything you sell.

questions.q: Tamika's first éclairs baked flat. What was the most likely cause?
o: The paste was too thin because she added all the egg at once
She baked the éclairs in a lined tray instead of a greased one
She used strong flour, which makes choux too tough to rise
She beat the flour into the hot water for too long
questions.why: Choux must be stiff enough to hold its shape. Add the egg a little at a time, and stop when the paste is smooth and drops slowly from the spoon.

questions.q: Why did the second tray sink a little after Tamika opened the door at 8 minutes?
o: The oven lost heat, so the egg in the paste cooked too fast and set
Cold air got to shells that were not yet set, and they collapsed
The steam escaped through the open door, so the paste dried out
The shells took in moisture from the kitchen air and went soft
questions.why: Choux shells are held up by steam until the crust sets. Opening the door early lets cold air in and makes them sink, so keep it shut at first and bake until the shells are dry.

questions.q: Why must Tamika cool the paste a little before she beats in the egg?
o: Cold paste makes the finished éclairs taste better
Warm paste makes the flour go lumpy as the egg goes in
Hot paste starts to cook and scramble the egg
Hot paste makes the egg too thin to hold its shape
questions.why: If the paste is too hot, the egg begins to cook as it goes in and forms threads, spoiling the smooth paste. Cool it for a few minutes first.

questions.q: Tamika leaves the filled éclairs on the bench from 11:30 to 12:30 in a 30 °C kitchen. What is the problem?
o: The cream will pick up the taste of the warm pastry
The pastry will go too hard and dry to eat
The cream is in the danger zone, where germs grow fast
The chocolate on top will crack as the éclairs cool down
questions.why: Pastry cream and whipped cream are high-risk foods. They must be kept covered at 5 °C or below until service, not warm in the danger zone.

questions.q: The butter has gone soft and greasy while Marlon rolls. What is the best thing to do?
o: Roll faster, so that the butter has less time to soften
Sprinkle a good deal of flour on the bench and continue
Wrap the pastry and chill it for about 20 minutes
Fold the pastry again, so that the warm butter spreads evenly through it
questions.why: Warm butter melts into the dough and the layers are lost. Chilling firms the fat and relaxes the dough. More flour would only toughen the pastry.

questions.q: Why should Marlon rest the pastry in the fridge between the turns?
o: So the yeast has time to work
So the fat stays firm and the dough relaxes
So that the water can drain out of the dough
So that it will be easier to colour
questions.why: Chilling keeps the fat in separate layers instead of melting into the dough, and lets the gluten relax so that the pastry does not shrink.

questions.q: What probably made Marlon's cases rise lopsided?
o: A blunt cutter, and egg wash on the cut edges, glued the layers
A sharp cutter pressed straight down squashed the edges of the cases
A very hot oven made the layers rise before the pastry had set
The pastry was rolled evenly, so the steam could not escape from it
questions.why: A blunt cutter squashes the edges, and egg wash on them glues the layers together, so one side rises and the other does not. Cut straight down with a sharp cutter and glaze the top only.

questions.q: A recipe for short pastry needs 300 g of fat, which is half the weight of the flour. How much flour is needed?
questions.why: Fat is half the weight of the flour, so the flour is twice the fat: 2 x 300 g = 600 g.

questions.q: A fruit tart has a layer of almond paste under the fruit. Which allergen must be added to its label, besides wheat and milk?
o: Nuts
Sesame
Soya
Celery
questions.why: Almond paste is made from ground almonds, so the tart contains nuts. Guests with a nut allergy can react seriously, so list it on the label and keep the tart apart from nut-free items.
